4-1.title: Consistent Verb Tense
4-1.learn:
HOW TO KEEP VERB TENSE CONSISTENT

Tense shows WHEN something happens: past (walked), present (walks), or future (will walk). Keep your verbs in the SAME time frame unless the timing really changes.

Example 1 — Inconsistent: 'She walks into the room and grabbed her coat.'
'Walks' is present, but 'grabbed' is past. They don't match. Fix to all past: 'She walked into the room and grabbed her coat.' OR all present: 'She walks into the room and grabs her coat.'

Example 2 — Consistent past: 'He opened the door, looked outside, and smiled.'
All three verbs (opened, looked, smiled) are past tense, so it flows.

Example 3 — When a change IS okay: 'Yesterday I studied, and tomorrow I will take the test.'
Here the time really changes from past to future, so different tenses are correct.

To check: read your sentence and find every verb. If they bounce between past and present by accident, pick one tense and make them all match.

4-2.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
4-2.learn:
HOW TO MAKE SUBJECTS AND VERBS AGREE

A SINGULAR subject needs a singular verb; a PLURAL subject needs a plural verb. In present tense, a singular verb often ends in -s, while the plural form does not.

Example 1 — 'The dog runs.' / 'The dogs run.'
One dog = 'runs' (singular verb). Many dogs = 'run' (plural verb).

Example 2 — Watch for words BETWEEN the subject and verb: 'The box of crayons IS on the desk.'
The subject is 'box' (singular), NOT 'crayons.' So the verb is 'is,' not 'are.' Ignore the prepositional phrase 'of crayons' when choosing the verb.

Example 3 — Compound subjects with 'and' are plural: 'Sam and Maria walk to school.'
Two people joined by 'and' take the plural verb 'walk.'

Tip: Find the TRUE subject first (cross out any 'of ___' phrases), decide if it's singular or plural, then match the verb.

4-3.title: Active vs. Passive Voice
4-3.learn:
HOW TO TELL ACTIVE FROM PASSIVE VOICE

In ACTIVE voice, the subject DOES the action: 'The chef cooked the meal.' (chef = doer, comes first)
In PASSIVE voice, the subject RECEIVES the action: 'The meal was cooked by the chef.' (meal = receiver, doer comes last or is missing)

Example 1 — Active: 'The dog chased the ball.'
The subject 'dog' does the chasing. Strong and direct.

Example 2 — Passive: 'The ball was chased by the dog.'
The subject 'ball' receives the action. It uses a 'be' verb (was) + past participle (chased), often with 'by.'

Example 3 — Spotting passive: look for a form of 'be' (is, was, were, been) + a past-participle verb, and ask 'who did it?' If the doer comes after 'by' (or is missing), it's passive.
Active: 'Maria wrote the letter.' Passive: 'The letter was written by Maria.'
Active voice is usually clearer and stronger, so prefer it in most writing.

questions.question: Which sentence is in ACTIVE voice?

choices.B: The cake was eaten by the kids.

questions.explanation: In 'The kids ate the cake,' the subject 'kids' does the action, so it is active.

questions.question: Which sentence is in PASSIVE voice?

choices.B: The mural was painted by the artist.
choices.D: The artist will paint a mural.

questions.explanation: In 'The mural was painted by the artist,' the subject 'mural' receives the action, so it is passive.

questions.question: In active voice, what does the subject do?
questions.explanation: In active voice, the subject performs or does the action.

questions.question: Which is the ACTIVE version of 'The window was broken by the storm.'?

choices.D: The storm was broken by the window.

questions.explanation: Making the doer 'the storm' the subject creates the active sentence 'The storm broke the window.'

questions.question: Which is the PASSIVE version of 'The teacher graded the tests.'?

choices.C: The tests were graded by the teacher.

questions.explanation: Making the receiver 'the tests' the subject creates the passive 'The tests were graded by the teacher.'

questions.question: What clue helps you spot passive voice?

choices.A: A form of 'be' (is, was, were) plus a past-participle verb

questions.explanation: Passive voice uses a 'be' verb plus a past participle, often with 'by' naming the doer.

questions.question: Which sentence is ACTIVE?

choices.B: The package was delivered by the driver.

questions.explanation: In 'The driver delivered the package,' the subject 'driver' performs the action, making it active.

questions.question: Why is active voice usually preferred?

choices.C: It hides who did the action.

questions.explanation: Active voice is usually clearer and more direct because the doer comes first.

4-4.title: Verb Mood
4-4.learn:
HOW TO IDENTIFY VERB MOOD

Mood shows the PURPOSE of a verb. The three main moods are:
INDICATIVE — states a fact or asks a question: 'It is raining.' / 'Are you ready?'
IMPERATIVE — gives a command or request: 'Close the window.' (The subject 'you' is understood.)
SUBJUNCTIVE — shows a wish or something not real/contrary to fact: 'If I were taller, I'd dunk.' Notice 'were,' not 'was,' in a wish.

Example 1 — Indicative: 'The sun rises in the east.'
It simply states a fact, so the mood is indicative.

Example 2 — Imperative: 'Please sit down.'
It gives a command. The subject 'you' is understood, so the mood is imperative.

Example 3 — Subjunctive: 'I wish I were a bird.'
It expresses a wish about something untrue. The subjunctive uses 'were' (not 'was') even with 'I.'
Key clue: commands = imperative; facts/questions = indicative; wishes or 'if I were' = subjunctive.

4-5.title: Verbals: Gerunds, Infinitives & Participles
4-5.learn:
HOW TO RECOGNIZE VERBALS

Verbals are verb forms that act as OTHER parts of speech. There are three kinds:
GERUND — ends in -ing and acts as a NOUN: 'Swimming is fun.' (Swimming is the subject, a noun.)
INFINITIVE — is 'to + verb' and often acts as a noun: 'I want to swim.' (to swim = what I want)
PARTICIPLE — a verb form (often -ing or -ed) that acts as an ADJECTIVE to describe a noun: 'the swimming pool,' 'the broken cup.'

Example 1 — Gerund: 'Running keeps me healthy.'
'Running' ends in -ing and acts as a noun (the subject), so it is a gerund.

Example 2 — Infinitive: 'She loves to read.'
'To read' is 'to + verb' and names what she loves, so it is an infinitive.

Example 3 — Participle: 'The barking dog scared me.'
'Barking' describes the noun 'dog,' so it is a participle (acting as an adjective).

Key test: Is the -ing word a NOUN (gerund) or describing a noun (participle)? Is it 'to + verb' (infinitive)?

questions.explanation: 'To learn' is 'to + verb,' which makes it an infinitive.

questions.explanation: 'Broken' is a participle describing the noun 'window,' acting like an adjective.
